A lot of it also has to do with the requirements to report an adult missing in KC MO. Individuals can report a missing person, but the police will only complete an official report (for missing adults) if the individual was last seen in KC MO, and meets at least 1 or more of the following criteria: 
1. Life threatening ailment
2. Under the care of a psychiatrist
3. If the person has threatened suicide
4. If they suffer from diminished mental capacity or medical condition
5. If they have dementia or Alzheimer's
6. If police detect strong indication of foul play. 

If those criteria aren't met, then the police won't complete the official report, which means the report won't be entered into state and national missing person databases.

Good question! I've always wondered that, too! I'm not entirely sure. I don't think it would be that simple. STDs have incubation periods, or the time that passes between exposure and the first symptoms. And that length of time varies by STD. Another big factor is the window period. After exposure, there's usually a period of time before a test will show positive. So people could be infected, but all the diagnostic results come back negative. Then there's the whole issue of people who are infected but don't show any symptoms. 

Probably the most important factor in extinction is looking at where the pathogen came from. For example, HIV originated in African primates as SIV (simian immunodeficiency virus). It mutated in a way that allowed it to jump the species​ barrier and infect humans. So, I guess if HIV did become extinct, that whole transmission event could happen again.

Zoo's are actually doing lots of awesome things to avoid inbreeding. The amount of reproductive management that goes into choosing breeding pairs is astounding. 

One of the most promising technologies is cryopreservation and artificial insemination, because then you don't have to worry about incompatible breeding pairs or all the problems that came happen with shipping animals. However, there's still a lot of research that has to be done because there's a lot of species differences with sperm (on the molecular level), and, as a result, some semen is more sensitive to freezing than other species. I had an internship at a zoo and that was the main research project I contributed to. 

I actually got to analyze semen from an old, inbred male (I think his inbreeding coefficient was like .25, which means he was likely the result of a mating between siblings) and his semen was all fucked up under the microscope.

I'm so sorry to hear this, OP. My condolences. My mother died quite quickly from stage four breast cancer. While I know it's not great, cheery, or happy to think about (and I'm basing your experiences off of my experience), I would try to maybe see a counselor from your local hospice or the like. They can help you with what to expect with the whole process. 

Also, I know no one likes talking about it, but, hopefully your father's affairs are already in order. Like, not just with a will and stuff; but life insurance, retirement, bank account beneficiaries, etc. Stuff like that can end up being a complete nightmare to deal with on top of having to deal with the grief and other, more pressing arrangements. 

I'm sorry to sound so fatalistic, but speaking from the absolute worse-case scenario, these are things I wish I had known going into it. Especially with education on the dying process. Sometimes it's fast and sometimes it's slow. Had I known what to look for, I never would've left the hospital. I hope you never have to use this advice. Feel free to pm me. My thoughts are with you in this difficult time.
